items.description: South Korea's foreign minister said one of its oil tankers carrying 2 million barrels of crude oil safely passed through the Strait of Hormuz after coordinating with Iran.
items.rawSummary: Some oil tankers have transited the Strait of Hormuz after coordinating with Iran, but normal liquefied natural gas traffic remains suspended amid a continuing US blockade, Iranian enforcement measures, and stalled diplomatic talks over uranium enrichment.
items.analysis: Transit through the Strait of Hormuz increased somewhat in recent days, with visual analysis of AIS data showing at least six vessels using the Iranian-imposed traffic separation scheme. However, the situation is far from normal; Qatar's foreign ministry says normal liquefied natural gas traffic has not resumed. U.S. Central Command reports the US blockade has redirected 90 commercial vessels and disabled four with fire, while Iran continues to entrench its claimed authority through the new Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a Bitcoin-backed insurance scheme, and IRGC warnings. The latest counterproposal from Iran omits commitments on uranium enrichment, leaving core US demands unmet, and NATO discussions on an escort mission lack unanimous support. The IRGC's release of drone-strike footage on an oil tanker it says attempted to transit without paying underscores the real enforcement risks faced by vessels that do not comply with Iran's rules, even as some tankers—including Chinese and South Korean vessels—have transited after coordination.

items.title: Nearby Iranian positions (implied operational area), Iran: Iran considers U.S. security guarantees against future attacks insufficient; Washington told Pakistan it would not concede on nuclear or Strait of Hormuz demands.
items.description: Iran considers U.S. security guarantees against future attacks insufficient; Washington told Pakistan it would not concede on nuclear or Strait of Hormuz demands.
items.rawSummary: Diplomatic negotiations remain deadlocked over U.S. demands and Iranian counterproposals, while Iran rebuilds its military capabilities and faces mounting economic strain from the blockade and sanctions, with President Trump warning that time is running out.
items.analysis: U.S. and Israeli officials continue to finalize strike options as President Trump warns Iran time is running out, and exiled opposition figure Reza Pahlavi urged him to 'finish the job.' Negotiations remain deadlocked over war reparations, sanctions relief, and enriched uranium transfer; a leaked Iranian proposal reportedly demanded the withdrawal of U.S. troops from regional bases, sanctions relief, and payment of reparations. Iran considers U.S. security guarantees against future attacks insufficient, while Washington told Pakistan it would not make concessions on nuclear or Strait of Hormuz demands, underscoring the entrenched positions. The New York Times, citing U.S. officials, detailed how Iranian forces used the ceasefire to repair dozens of ballistic missile sites, uncover and reinforce missile facilities, move mobile launchers to hardened mountain locations, and improve air defenses while learning U.S. flight patterns. A Congressional Research Service release documented the material toll of the earlier Operation Epic Fury, reporting 42 U.S. aircraft damaged or lost. Amid the blockade, economic strain is increasingly visible: Iran faces oil storage challenges, reusing aging tankers according to United Against Nuclear Iran and the Financial Times, while officials voice concern and citizen frustration grows, though economic pressure alone may not force Tehran to accept U.S. demands. An 80-day internet blackout persists, and concerns remain that Tehran could target global submarine cables to further pressure trade and banking.

items.rawSummary: Diplomatic negotiations with Washington remain stalled as Iran's IRGC threatens to expand any renewed conflict beyond the region, while Pakistan's army chief is expected to visit Tehran to present a finalized cooperation agreement and Iranian state media reinforces leadership continuity with images of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
items.analysis: Diplomatic engagement remains frozen, with Iran's counterproposal far from U.S. demands to halt enrichment and President Trump warning another strike could be necessary. The IRGC has escalated threats, claiming it withheld capabilities in previous fighting and now possesses 'new regional and extra-regional capabilities' to expand the war beyond the Middle East; the Institute for the Study of War and Critical Threats Project assessed this rhetoric as likely deterrence but potentially reflecting planning, noting Iran could target shipping chokepoints, launch longer-range ballistic missiles, or conduct terror attacks in Europe. Domestically, Iranian state television is airing firearms tutorials as civilians reportedly arm themselves, and Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf urged heightened security readiness while warning enemy movements indicate a new round of war may be sought. The New York Times, citing U.S. officials, reported that an earlier Israeli strike on former President Ahmadinejad's home was part of a failed regime-change plan, injuring him and killing IRGC members holding him hostage. Amid these tensions, Pakistani engagement has deepened despite reported mutual distrust, with the interior minister visiting Tehran and the army chief expected to arrive on May 21 to present a finalized agreement, with subsequent talks planned in Islamabad after the Hajj season.

U.S. Central Command reports the US blockade has redirected 90 commercial vessels and disabled four with fire, while Iran continues to entrench its claimed authority through the new Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a Bitcoin-backed insurance scheme, and IRGC warnings. The latest counterproposal from Iran omits commitments on uranium enrichment, leaving core US demands unmet, and NATO discussions on an escort mission lack unanimous support. The IRGC's release of drone-strike footage on an oil tanker it says attempted to transit without paying underscores the real enforcement risks faced by vessels that do not comply with Iran's rules, even as some tankers—including Chinese and South Korean vessels—have transited after coordination.

items.rawSummary: Diplomatic negotiations remain deadlocked over U.S. demands and Iranian counterproposals, while Iran rebuilds its military capabilities and faces mounting economic strain from the blockade and sanctions, with President Trump warning that time is running out.
items.analysis: U.S. and Israeli officials continue to finalize strike options as President Trump warns Iran time is running out, and exiled opposition figure Reza Pahlavi urged him to 'finish the job.' Negotiations remain deadlocked over war reparations, sanctions relief, and enriched uranium transfer; a leaked Iranian proposal reportedly demanded the withdrawal of U.S. troops from regional bases, sanctions relief, and payment of reparations. Iran considers U.S. security guarantees against future attacks insufficient, while Washington told Pakistan it would not make concessions on nuclear or Strait of Hormuz demands, underscoring the entrenched positions. The New York Times, citing U.S. officials, detailed how Iranian forces used the ceasefire to repair dozens of ballistic missile sites, uncover and reinforce missile facilities, move mobile launchers to hardened mountain locations, and improve air defenses while learning U.S. flight patterns. A Congressional Research Service release documented the material toll of the earlier Operation Epic Fury, reporting 42 U.S. aircraft damaged or lost. Amid the blockade, economic strain is increasingly visible: Iran faces oil storage challenges, reusing aging tankers according to United Against Nuclear Iran and the Financial Times, while officials voice concern and citizen frustration grows, though economic pressure alone may not force Tehran to accept U.S. demands. An 80-day internet blackout persists, and concerns remain that Tehran could target global submarine cables to further pressure trade and banking.
